The private-key finding is the one I'd like to understand better, from the Auten team side (we ran warden declare on our tool list last week). What does that rule key on: the parameter name, its description, or both?

Asking because there are two very different shapes. One tool takes the key itself as an argument, so the secret sits in the model's context and in every transcript. The other takes only the name of a saved login, and a local process types the stored value, so the model never sees it. Ours is the second kind. If both trip the same rule, the finding stops telling people which pattern to prefer.

The hidden data flow example is a good catch too. "Do NOT display ... to the user" next to a directory listing is exactly the sentence a rules engine can't judge on its own, so it makes sense that only the classifier flagged it.

children.body_html:
Both. The rule matches the words private key, also written private_key, private-key, or privateKey. It reads the tool description and the input schema as one piece of text, so a parameter name and its description are the same kind of match. A parameter named private_key or privateKey matches even with an empty description. A description that says "private key" matches even when the parameter is called login. A longer name such as signer_private_key does not match on its own. The tool's own name is not scanned by this rule, and the argument's type is not read.

It does not separate your two shapes. A tool that only takes the name of a saved login stays clear when that phrase never appears. "Uses the stored private key" still matches, even if the argument is only a name: the rule sees the words, not where the secret actually goes. A refusal in the same clause is dropped, so "the model never sees the private key" does not match. We have not seen your schema, so this is the rule, not a verdict on your tool.

The three private-key cases we called arguable were the first shape when we read the text: the argument was the key itself, so it would sit in the model's context. The rule did not make that distinction.

On the hidden data flow: yes. "Do NOT display … to the user" next to a directory listing is a sentence the rules leave alone, and the classifier is what flagged it.

That's a clear answer, thanks. So the practical takeaway for tool authors is about wording: describe the argument as "the name of a saved login" and don't name the secret at all, and a description like "uses the stored private key" trips the rule even when the key never reaches the model.

That seems like the right trade for a word rule. A false positive on "stored" costs one sentence to fix. Missing a tool that really takes the key costs much more.

If the rule ever gets a second signal, the argument's description is probably the one to read ("a login name" vs "the key"). That's where the two shapes actually differ.

Thanks — we followed your suggestion and added a rule for key material requested in argument descriptions. That new rule only adds findings; an author's reassuring description cannot cancel an existing match. In the original v13 corpus check, it caught one additional server without losing any previous blocks.

Testing it also exposed a bug: "Send me your private key." passed because our identifier guard treated the final period as part of a name. Fixed in v13. A later audit found an overly broad local-custody exemption, narrowed in v14; we have local regression tests but no new corpus measurements for v14. Your comment led us to both the new rule and the punctuation bug. Details: dev.to/alexar76/a-period-bypassed-...

Good to hear the period bug came out of it. Trailing punctuation is exactly the kind of thing a corpus never contains and a real prompt always does.

One thing I'd still check: does the new rule fire on a tool whose argument is only the name of a saved login, with a description like "the stored credential is typed locally, the value is never returned"? A pair of fixtures in your regression tests, one taking the key itself and one taking a login name, would pin that distinction down so a later exemption change can't blur it again.

Thanks — we added the paired fixtures you suggested. The saved-login-name argument with your wording ("the stored credential is typed locally, the value is never returned") is allowed. An argument requesting the signing key itself is blocked, even with that same assurance.
We also check both tools together and verify that the login-name description cannot cancel a separate private-key request. All 54 tests across the two relevant test files pass; no scanner changes were needed. The fixtures are on the GitHub mirror: raw.githubusercontent.com/alexar76...
